newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says NATO, Russia heading for deal.
newsitem.headline: France says NATO, Russia heading for deal.

text.p: France on Saturday hailed the summit between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin as showing NATO and Russia were on track for a deal to defuse Moscow's opposition to NATO expansion.
"It seems that the talks between the two presidents confirmed that we are on the path to a deal between NATO and Russia," French Defence Minister Charles Millon told Europe 1 radio.

"Such an accord is important because it will allow us to go beyond Yalta and to guarantee European stability...and avoid a state of confrontation," he said. The Yalta summit at the end of World War Two led to the Cold War division of Europe.
At their Helsinki summit on Friday the two presidents agreed to differ over NATO's expansion plans but vowed to press ahead with a charter defining a new relationship between Moscow and the alliance.
Yeltsin's communist foes in Russia branded the outcome a capitulation.

Clinton brushed aside Russian objections to NATO enlargement into eastern Europe, declaring it would go ahead as planned at a NATO summit in July when Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to be invited to join.
"We must continue to explain to (Yeltsin) that the reform of the Atlantic Alliance, its enlargement, aim to reinforce the security of the European continent," Millon said.
After the Cold War, "there is no longer a split in Europe...merely a whole that we all safeguard," he added.
Millon is to travel to Washington on Monday for talks with Defence Secretary William Cohen to try to resolve Paris' own disputes with the United States about NATO reform.

Paris wants a European officer to take over from an American at the head of the Naples-based Southern Command of NATO as the price of its return to NATO's military wing after three decades. Washington has refused.
"France has always been very clear," Millon said. "If there is no progress on this point, France will remain at its current status."
"But we expect that we can reach points of accord after discussions and dialogue with our American friends," he added.
